meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to work', paired with 'поработать'.

examples.trans: I work as mayor.
Where do you work?

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's what you said.
That house is old.
Well, the thing you said.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'лгода'). Common masculine noun meaning 'half a year, six months' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: In six months.
I've been here for six months now.

examples.text: Ты эти деньги через полгода вернёшь.
examples.trans: You'll get this money back in six months.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'казывать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to order', paired with 'заказать'.

examples.trans: Call and order pizza!
What will you order?

examples.text: Ладно, звони в свою пиццу. Заказывай!
examples.trans: All right, call your pizza place. Go ahead and order!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'zucchini' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I ordered zucchini.
Do you call this zucchini?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem '-твоий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('wife').

examples.text: То есть я, по-твоему, плохая жена?
examples.trans: So in your opinion, am I a bad wife?

examples.text: Вика, не проще яйца без скорлупы добавить?
examples.trans: Vika, wouldn't it be simpler to add eggs without the shells?

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'kids; guys' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.
Then the boys will have a little word with you.
Right, kids, go out of the room.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'быть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to forget', paired with 'забывать'.

examples.trans: Don't forget to wash the toilet.
I forgot the keys.

examples.text: Сейчас будешь чинить трубу. И унитаз не забудь помыть.
examples.trans: Now you're going to fix the pipe. And don't forget to wash the toilet.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'менить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to replace', paired with 'заменять'.

examples.trans: We demand that house arrest be replaced.
Who will replace me tomorrow?

examples.text: Мы требуем заменить домашний арест. Нужна подписка о невыезде.
examples.trans: We demand that house arrest be replaced. What's needed is a travel ban.

meanings.note: Agent noun formed with the international suffix '-ист' denoting a specialist or adherent. Common masculine noun meaning '86'd list, out-of-stock menu list' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Guys, I forgot to update the eighty-six list.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый стоп-лист.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new 86'd list.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.
Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.
Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'place; seat' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is my seat.
It's a nice place here.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'дурок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'fool, moron, jerk' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are only morons around!

examples.text: Вокруг меня одни лентяи и придурки!
examples.trans: Around me are only slackers and fools!

examples.text: Ну ты и придурок, честное слово!
examples.trans: Well you are a jerk, honestly!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'fish' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: A big platter of fish and crabs.

examples.text: На ужин мы приготовили свежую рыбу.
examples.trans: For dinner we cooked fresh fish.

examples.text: У нас есть большая тарелка рыбы и крабов.
examples.trans: We have a big platter of fish and crabs.

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'делывать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to butcher, dress'.

examples.trans: The chef learns to butcher meat.

examples.text: Каждый повар обязан уметь разделывать мясо.
examples.trans: Every chef is obliged to know how to butcher meat.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'прашивать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to ask', paired with 'спросить'.

examples.trans: I'm asking you!
He always asks.

examples.text: Вот это что такое, я вас спрашиваю!
examples.trans: What is this, I'm asking you!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'volunteer, person wishing to' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Yet there are plenty of people eager to get hired too.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый желающий.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new volunteer.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'строиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to get a job, settle'.

examples.trans: To get a job.

examples.text: Кем вы хотите устроиться на работу?
examples.trans: What job do you want to get?
Nice, you have set yourself up very well!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'too, also', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Me too.
He's here too.

examples.text: Мы же здесь выросли. И о людях тоже надо думать.
examples.trans: After all, we grew up here. And you have to think about people too.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to grab, to seize', paired with 'схватить'.

examples.trans: Why is he grabbing me?
Don't grab me!

examples.text: Почему он меня всё время за горло хватает?
examples.trans: Why does he keep grabbing me by the throat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'one', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Give me just one.
I have one brother.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to leave, to go away', paired with 'уйти'.

examples.trans: I'm going home.
You are. Go away.
I'm leaving.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').

examples.trans: Could we go somewhere else?
That's a different building.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to come', paired with 'прийти'.

examples.trans: Come tomorrow.
He comes every day.
If you change your mind, come back. The job is waiting.
